## Introduction

This tutorial covers key concepts from [Chapter 7: Data Import](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-import.html), [Chapter 18: Missing Values](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/missing-values.html), and [Chapter 10: Exploratory Data Analysis](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html) from [*R for Data Science (2e)*](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/) by Hadley Wickham, Mine Çetinkaya-Rundel, and Garrett Grolemund.

You will use AI to explore a sample of the Million Song Dataset: a plain CSV that looks complete at first glance and turns out to be missing most of what it claims to hold. Your job is to steer the analysis, render often, inspect the output, and decide what the data can honestly show.

Use AI however you like.

###

A CSV is the plainest possible table: one line per row, values separated by commas, and a first line naming the columns.

```
"artist.name","artist.familiarity","song.year"
"Casual",0.581793766,0
"The Box Tops",0.630630038,1969
```

No types, no formulas, no formatting — which is exactly why every programming language, database, and spreadsheet program can read one.

## Million Song Dataset

The **music** CSV file comes from a teaching version of the [Million Song Dataset](https://corgis-edu.github.io/corgis/csv/music/) published by CORGIS. It includes 10,000 rows and 35 columns about artists, songs, and audio features — more than you can scan at a glance — so the first step is understanding what is in it.

`read_csv()` guessed a type for each of those 35 columns and converted 350,000 values, and its guesses are worth checking. This file uses the number `0` for "we don't know", even in columns that ought to hold text, so `artist.location` and `song.title` come back as `<dbl>` rather than `<chr>`.

###

The dotted naming convention groups variables by entity: `artist.*` columns describe the performer, `release.*` columns describe the album, and `song.*` columns describe the track. When asking AI to work with a specific column, using its exact name — `artist.hotttnesss`, not just `hotness` — prevents AI from guessing the wrong column.

Look at the values, not just the names: `artist.name` and `artist.terms` are populated, but `artist.location`, `song.title`, and half the `song.year` values are `0`. A column that exists is not the same as a column you can use.

### Exercise 9

Find out what `artist.familiarity` and `artist.hotttnesss` measure — the [dataset documentation](https://corgis-edu.github.io/corgis/csv/music/) is one good source.

Describe what each one measures below.

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-9
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Find out what artist.familiarity and artist.hotttnesss measure — the dataset documentation at https://corgis-edu.github.io/corgis/csv/music/ is one good source. Describe what each one measures below.",
  learnr2::answer("`artist.familiarity` estimates how well known an artist is. `artist.hotttnesss` estimates how much buzz or current popularity an artist has.", correct = TRUE),
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

Both variables run from 0 to 1, where higher values mean more familiarity or more hotness. They are related but not identical: an artist can be widely known without being especially hot at that moment, or newly hot without being familiar to everyone. Nonpositive values should be treated as missing rather than as real zeros.

### Exercise 10

Get summary statistics — minimum, maximum, median, and quartiles — for `artist.familiarity`, `artist.hotttnesss`, `song.year`, and `song.tempo`. Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-10-answer
#| echo: true
music |>
  select(artist.familiarity, artist.hotttnesss, song.year, song.tempo) |>
  summary()
```

###

Notice the minimums: `song.year` has a minimum of 0, which is not a real release year, and `artist.familiarity` and `artist.hotttnesss` have values at or near 0 that represent missing or unusable data rather than genuinely zero-familiarity artists. Scanning the minimum and maximum of each numeric column is a fast way to spot placeholder values and understand the scale before plotting.

### Exercise 11

The summary didn't give a clear picture of the distribution of song years. Plot the distribution of `song.year`, filtering out rows where `song.year` is 0, and include the number of songs used in the subtitle. Render and take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-11
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "The summary didn't give a clear picture of the distribution of song years. Plot the distribution of song.year, filtering out rows where song.year is 0, and include the number of songs used in the subtitle. Render and take a screenshot of the plot in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-11-answer
#| echo: true
music |>
  filter(song.year > 0) |>
  ggplot(aes(x = song.year)) +
  geom_histogram(binwidth = 5, fill = "steelblue", color = "white") +
  labs(
    title = "Distribution of songs by release year",
    subtitle = "n = 4,680 songs with a recorded release year",
    x = "Release year",
    y = "Number of songs",
    caption = "Source: Million Song Dataset (teaching sample)"
  )
```

###

The dataset skews heavily toward recent music: over half the songs are from the 2000s, with a long tail of older recordings going back to the 1920s. The n = 4,680 in the subtitle is much smaller than the 10,000 rows in the file, because 53% of the songs carry a placeholder year of 0.

### Exercise 12

We know from earlier that several other columns also use placeholders. Count how many rows have placeholder values in `artist.location`, `release.name`, `song.title`, `song.year`, `artist.familiarity`, and `artist.hotttnesss`. For the numeric scores, treat any value of 0 as a placeholder. Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-12
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "We know from earlier that several other columns also use placeholders. Count how many rows have placeholder values in artist.location, release.name, song.title, song.year, artist.familiarity, and artist.hotttnesss. For the numeric scores, treat any value of 0 as a placeholder. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-12-answer
#| echo: true
music |>
  summarise(
    rows = n(),
    artist_location_zero = sum(artist.location == "0" | is.na(artist.location)),
    release_name_zero = sum(release.name == "0" | is.na(release.name)),
    song_title_zero = sum(song.title == "0" | is.na(song.title)),
    song_year_zero = sum(song.year == 0 | is.na(song.year)),
    familiarity_zero = sum(artist.familiarity <= 0, na.rm = TRUE),
    hotttnesss_zero = sum(artist.hotttnesss <= 0, na.rm = TRUE)
  )
```

###

Missingness in this file is wildly uneven: `artist.location` (9,999), `song.title` (9,992), and `release.name` (9,989) are placeholders in nearly every one of the 10,000 rows, so those columns are useless no matter what you ask of them. `artist.familiarity` has only 24 zero values (less than 1%) while `artist.hotttnesss` has 496 (nearly 5%).

### Exercise 13

Artist locations are also stored as latitude and longitude. Make a world map showing every artist's location, exactly as the file records it, using the **[maps](https://cran.r-project.org/package=maps)** package for the world background.

Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-18
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Artist locations are also stored as latitude and longitude. Make a world map showing every artist's location, exactly as the file records it, using the maps package for the world background. Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-18-answer
#| echo: true
world <- map_data("world")

music |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_map(
    data = world, map = world,
    aes(map_id = region),
    fill = "gray90", color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = artist.longitude, y = artist.latitude),
    alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue", size = 0.6
  ) +
  expand_limits(x = world$long, y = world$lat) +
  labs(
    title = "Artist locations in the Million Song Dataset",
    subtitle = "One point per song, plotted exactly as the file records it",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Million Song Dataset teaching CSV"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

###

Most of the points sit in a single blob in the Gulf of Guinea, off the west coast of Africa, where the equator crosses the prime meridian — latitude 0, longitude 0, a spot sometimes called Null Island. No artist lives there; that is where every unknown location landed.

### Exercise 14

Count how many songs (rows) have usable coordinates versus placeholder coordinates, where placeholder means both latitude and longitude equal 0. Render. In the R Terminal, run `show_file("analysis.qmd", chunk = "Last")`. CP/CR.

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-13
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Count how many songs (rows) have usable coordinates versus placeholder coordinates, where placeholder means both latitude and longitude equal 0. Render. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"analysis.qmd\", chunk = \"Last\"). CP/CR.",
  type = "reflection",
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-13-answer
#| echo: true
music |>
  summarise(
    total = n(),
    placeholder_coords = sum(artist.latitude == 0 & artist.longitude == 0),
    usable_coords = sum(!(artist.latitude == 0 & artist.longitude == 0))
  )
```

###

6,258 of the 10,000 rows (63%) sit at (0, 0), so the blob held most of the data and the rest of the map was drawn from the other 3,742. Storing "unknown" as 0 rather than `NA` is a classic data-quality trap, because 0 is a perfectly valid coordinate and nothing in the file marks those rows as missing.

### Exercise 15

Iterate the map. Filter out artists where both latitude and longitude equal 0, and add a title and subtitle that note the coverage limitation.

Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-14
#| echo: false
learnr2::question(
  "Iterate the map. Filter out artists where both latitude and longitude equal 0, and add a title and subtitle that note the coverage limitation. Take a screenshot of the map in your rendered page and paste it below.",
  type = "reflection",
  allow_image = TRUE,
  show_text = FALSE
)
```

###

```{r}
#| label: million-song-dataset-14-answer
#| echo: true
world <- map_data("world")

music |>
  filter(!(artist.latitude == 0 & artist.longitude == 0)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_map(
    data = world, map = world,
    aes(map_id = region),
    fill = "gray90", color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = artist.longitude, y = artist.latitude),
    alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue", size = 0.6
  ) +
  expand_limits(x = world$long, y = world$lat) +
  labs(
    title = "Artist locations in the Million Song Dataset",
    subtitle = "Only 37% of artists have usable coordinates; US and Western Europe dominate",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Million Song Dataset teaching CSV"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```

###

The map reveals a strong geographic bias: most artists with usable coordinates are from the United States and Western Europe. Maps built on incomplete location data are still useful — they show where the data is and is not, which is itself an analytical finding.

###

The Echo Nest, the company whose API produced these familiarity and hotness scores, was bought by Spotify in 2014 and its public API shut down two years later. `artist.hotttnesss` is therefore a snapshot of buzz from before the dataset's 2011 release, and it can never be refreshed.

## Summary

This tutorial used AI to explore a sample of the Million Song Dataset, drawing on [Chapter 7: Data Import](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/data-import.html), [Chapter 18: Missing Values](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/missing-values.html), and [Chapter 10: Exploratory Data Analysis](https://r4ds.hadley.nz/EDA.html) of *R for Data Science (2e)*. You downloaded and parsed a CSV file, cached the parse so it runs once per change, looked up what the familiarity and hotness scores measure, discovered that the file uses 0 for "unknown" in text columns, release years, and coordinates, mapped the artists and watched the unknown ones pile up at Null Island, then filtered them out for an honest map of where the data comes from.

  "Render. Check the rendered HTML. The page should be attractive, with clean versions of your plots. In the R Terminal, run show_file(\"analysis.qmd\"). CP/CR.",

###

````{verbatim}
---
title: "Million Song Dataset"
author: <your name>
execute:
  echo: false
---

```{r}
#| message: false
library(tidyverse)
library(maps)
```

```{r}
#| cache: true
music <- read_csv("data/music.csv", show_col_types = FALSE)
```

```{r}
world <- map_data("world")

music |>
  filter(!(artist.latitude == 0 & artist.longitude == 0)) |>
  ggplot() +
  geom_map(
    data = world, map = world,
    aes(map_id = region),
    fill = "gray90", color = "gray70", linewidth = 0.2
  ) +
  geom_point(
    aes(x = artist.longitude, y = artist.latitude),
    alpha = 0.3, color = "steelblue", size = 0.6
  ) +
  expand_limits(x = world$long, y = world$lat) +
  labs(
    title = "Artist locations in the Million Song Dataset",
    subtitle = "Only 37% of artists have usable coordinates; US and Western Europe dominate",
    x = NULL,
    y = NULL,
    caption = "Source: Million Song Dataset teaching CSV"
  ) +
  theme_minimal() +
  theme(axis.text = element_blank(), axis.ticks = element_blank())
```
````

###

Your page now tells one story: where the artists behind the Million Song sample are located, and how little of the sample that map can honestly include.
